grammar_sets.anchors_to: ChainAgnostic/CAIPs CAIP-2, CAIP-10, CAIP-19 identifier grammar
grammar_sets.cross_validated: 7-engine verdict agreement (2026-07-21, 102/102 each): Python, JavaScript(Node), Go(RE2), Rust(regex crate), Rust(no-regex hand parser), Java, PHP(PCRE), Ruby(Onigmo). Naive ^...$ over-acceptance measured per engine (Python 3, Java 8, PHP 3, Ruby 5, Go 0, Rust 0, JS 0; JS with m-flag 9, Rust with (?m) 5). See _attestations/2026-07-21-caip-edge-v1-seven-engine.md

grammar_note: Grammar sets pin identifier-level accept/reject verdicts for a chain-agnostic identifier grammar. They are NOT JCS canonicalisation vectors: they carry no per-vector canonical-bytes recompute, so they are NOT folded into total_anchor_sets / total_vectors. The conformance signal is verdict agreement across independent implementations over byte-identical inputs (corpus.tsv hex and caip_edge_v1.json base64 decode to the same bytes). Claim separation follows the adversarial-set rule: the input bytes are pinned, and the rejection verdicts are reference-implementation proof-of-record across the listed engines, not a canonical-byte claim.
parse_note: Parse sets pin accept/reject verdicts over RAW INPUT BYTES for defects that do not survive parsing, so they carry no per-vector canonical-bytes recompute and are NOT folded into total_anchor_sets / total_vectors. Same claim separation as grammar_sets. RFC 8785 canonicalises an already-parsed value, so a duplicate object member is gone before the canonicaliser runs: json.loads('{"a":1,"a":2}') yields {'a': 2}, and the canonical bytes of that parsed value verify for a document the raw input never unambiguously stated. RFC 8259 section 4 records three real divergent behaviours (last-only, parse error, report-all), which is why the check belongs at parse and why the verdict, not a canonical byte string, is the conformance signal. Reference-impl proof-of-record (Python object_pairs_hook); not cross-validated.
